lines.text: He picked his successor. Under three years later, he was back in the chair.
Then an activist came for a seat on the board. Three moves kept the board in control.
February 2020. Bob Iger hands Disney's CEO job to Bob Chapek.
Iger stays on as executive chairman until the end of 2021.
Less than a year after that, on Sunday, November 20, 2022, the board makes its move.
It announces that Chapek is out, and Iger is returning as CEO.
So how does a board pull off a switch like that?
Move number one: keep a proven replacement waiting in the wings.
Pushing out a CEO is a gamble, unless the replacement has done the job before.
Iger had.
Then, in January 2023, a new threat arrives: activist investor Nelson Peltz of Trian.
He launches a proxy fight for a seat on Disney's board.
Move number two: take away the other side's argument.
An activist needs a demand the company refuses. No refusal, no rally.
February 2023. Disney doesn't fight the demand. It does something stranger: it delivers it.
A restructuring, with about seven thousand job cuts and 5.5 billion dollars in cost savings.
Peltz demanded cuts. Disney made them. His argument is gone.
And Peltz drops the fight. Case closed? Not quite.
In 2024, Peltz comes back for another round.
This time, it goes all the way to a shareholder vote.
Move number three: win the vote by winning the big shareholders.
In a proxy fight, headlines make noise. Share counts decide.
Win the biggest holders, and the challenger has nowhere to go. So it all comes down to one count.
April 3, 2024. Disney shareholders cast their votes.
They vote Disney's whole board back in, and reject Peltz. He never gets his seat.
Three moves: a replacement waiting, an argument removed, the big holders won over.
Remove their reason to fight, and the fight ends.
Someone coming for your seat? Pull an Iger: leave them nothing to fight about. Practice that move with Deal Calm, on the App Store and at deal calm dot com.
